items.title: Motion to Reconvene into Open Session
Chris Gerrits, Re: Mannheim Water Capacity
notes:
C. Gerrits introduced himself and noted that he is representing the Waterloo Region Home Builders’ Association (WRHBA). He provided a list of his credentials, specifically B.Sc. (Eng) and M.Sc. in Water Resource Engineering (University of Guelph), and relevant experience with water systems in the Region of Waterloo. He recommended that the Region use the methodology provided in the 2015 Water Supply Master Plan as the water capacity resiliency factor in the proposed methodology is based on 20% of the system capacity instead of demand which results in an increase to the water deficit. He noted various construction freeze thresholds of comparable municipalities. He expressed concerns related to the implementation of the proposed methodology.

Responding to Council, C. Gerrits suggested that an in-depth analysis of previous processes, the potential use of offline wells, and establishing a second well, also known as twinning, which would provide some additional redundancy. He confirmed that staff have provided the requested data and the Region has a complex water system by design.

In response to Council, C. Gerrits explained that there are two (2) main considerations to the challenges with pumping water uphill from Middleton to Manheim, which are cost and secondary disinfection. He stated he believes there is capacity in the Cambridge aquifers to supply water to other areas.

Responding to Council, P. Law confirmed that all the suggestions from the presentation are being considered as part of the water supply strategy, and that the project to transfer water from the Middleton Service Area to the Mannheim Service Area is being considered on the expedited list.

In response to Council, P. Law clarified that the proposed methodology includes a resiliency target of 20% of the total system capacity, which will allow for planned and unplanned shutdowns. She further clarified that a framework looking into what level of risk and operational threshold the Region is willing to operate under to allow development will be brought back to Council on June 3, 2026.

Responding to a question from Council, Darshpreet Bhatti, Chief Administrative Officer, stated staff are aiming to publish this report a week prior to the meeting on June 3, 2026.

items.title: Board of Health Update
notes:
Dr. Hsiu-Li Wang, Commissioner of Public Health and Paramedic Services, provided an update on vector-borne and animal-borne diseases. H. Wang encouraged the public to take preventative measures over the summer months, including wearing light coloured clothing, long sleeves and pants, socks, and closed-toe shoes, as well as using insect repellant. H. Wang stated the Region of Waterloo has been designated as an established area for ticks, increasing the risk of Lyme disease. She encouraged the public to check for ticks after spending time outdoors.

H. Wang also discussed the risks of rabies, reminding the public to report all animal bites to Public Health. H. Wang stated more information about West Nile Virus, Lyme disease, and rabies can be found on the Region's website.

H. Wang provided an update on the strain of Hantavirus circulating on the MV Hondius cruise ship, stating that there are no known contacts residing in the Waterloo Region.

Council acknowledged the 25th Anniversary of Paramedic Services being operated by the Region. H. Wang noted an open house will be open to the public from 10-2pm at 1001A Erbs Road on May 23, 2026.

items.title: TSD-TRP-26-005, Ira Needles Blvd Resurfacing
notes:
Mathieu Goetzke, Commissioner of Transportation Services, provided a background on the recommendation to do a fulsome resurfacing of Ira Needles Boulevard for $4.5 million.

M. Goetzke emphasized that the funding for this project will come out of the Transportation Capital Reserve, which, unlike the Tax Stabilization Reserve, is funded annually to be able to fund renewal projects without incurring debt.

Responding to a question from Council, M. Goetzke explained that the cost of doing local repairs would be about $700,000, bring the total cost for this project up from $4.5 million to $5.2 million. He further explained that patch work maintenance would cost about $7 million over nine (9) years.

items.title: Councillor N. Salonen
notes:
N. Salonen introduced the motion and explained that the residents of Wilmot have expressed dissatisfaction with the current well interference policies. N. Salonen requested staff bring back a report to advise on a Council appointed Well Interference Committee, policy, and Terms of Reference.

Council discussed amendments to the motion to broaden the well area in which the motion speaks to, increasing public trust, and expanding the transparency section to also include monitoring data, complaint tracking, investigation reporting, and Committee recommendations. Council also discussed an amendment to include options for annual reporting of the number, status, and resolution of groundwater interference complaints, trends and mitigation methods.

Responding to Council, A. Shaw confirmed that staff are able to bring back a report detailing well interference complaints since 2015.

Responding to Council, A. Shaw stated that surface water impacts are often related to climate change or precipitation, and it would be difficult to address through this process. She also noted that surface water is outside of the jurisdiction of the Region.

K. Brothers explained that adequate time is needed to do a comprehensive review and come back with a wholesome report, as the proper consultations with stakeholders must take place.

Council discussed the timeline included in the motion.

motions.text: WHEREAS residents who rely on private wells must have access to a fair, transparent, evidence-based, and resident-centred process when they experience groundwater interference that may be connected to Regional water-taking activities; AND WHEREAS the Region’s current Policy and Procedures for Responding to Groundwater Interference Complaints , revised in April 2015, provides for Regional staff to investigate complaints and provides that appeals are heard by the Commissioner of Transportation and Environmental Services (now interim Commissioner of Water Services and Wastewater Operations); AND WHEREAS prior to the 2015 policy change, groundwater interference appeals in the Region of Waterloo were heard through a Council-appointed Well Interference Appeal Committee, formerly known as the Regional Water Liaison Committee; AND WHEREAS residents have raised concerns that the current process does not provide sufficient independence, transparency, or meaningful appeal from staff determinations, particularly where the Region is both the operator of the municipal wells and the body responsible for investigating and deciding complaints related to those wells; AND WHEREAS other Ontario municipalities, including the City of Guelph, maintain a Well Interference Committee model to hear appeals where a resident is dissatisfied with the municipality’s investigation, resolution, or compensation related to municipal groundwater taking; AND WHEREAS the City of Guelph’s Well Interference Committee model provides for a committee to review staff investigations, hear directly from affected well owners, consider municipal pumping data and well information, and recommend restoration or additional restoration where appropriate; AND WHEREAS the purpose of any well interference process should be to restore an adequate and reliable water supply to affected residents, rather than to limit the Region’s response to a fixed compensation amount that may not reflect the actual cost of restoration; AND WHEREAS residents in multiple areas of the Region have raised concerns regarding groundwater interference associated with municipal pumping activities; AND WHEREAS public confidence in groundwater management is strengthened through transparent, evidence-based, and arms-length review processes; THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT the Regional Municipality of Waterloo direct staff to bring forward a report and draft revised policy to the August 12, 2026 Special Council Water meeting to replace the current groundwater interference appeal process with a Council-appointed Well Interference Appeal Committee; AND THAT the revised policy and Terms of Reference be modelled on best practices from comparable municipal well interference appeal processes, including the City of Guelph model, and include the following: a) a mandate for the Committee to hear appeals from private well owners regarding groundwater interference complaints related to Regional water-taking activities; b) a process for the Committee to be convened where Regional staff determine that the Region is not responsible for a well interference complaint, where a resident is dissatisfied with the resolution offered, or where a resident is dissatisfied with the amount or form of compensation offered; c) a membership model that includes members of Regional Council and representatives from affected lower-tier municipalities, with consideration given to independent hydrogeological or technical expertise; d) a requirement that members hearing an appeal be independent from the staff responsible for the original investigation and recommendation; e) a process that allows affected residents to provide written materials, attend the hearing, present evidence, respond to staff findings, and answer questions from the Committee; f) a requirement that the Committee review all relevant information, including the location of the affected well relative to Regional wells, private well depth and water levels, municipal well details, municipal pumping data, water-level monitoring data, complaint history, investigation findings, and any mitigation measures taken to date; g) authority for the Committee to make recommendations to Regional Council respecting appropriate remedies, including temporary water supply, pump lowering, well deepening, new well drilling, connection to municipal water where feasible, abandonment of the old well where required, reimbursement of eligible costs, or other measures necessary to restore a reliable water supply; h) options to remove or revise the current $4,000 compensation limit where the evidence supports greater actual costs to restore an adequate water supply; i) options to ensure residents are not required to sign a full and final release of future claims before having access to a meaningful appeal process; j) enhanced public transparency respecting groundwater monitoring data, complaint tracking, investigation reporting, and Committee recommendations to Council, while protecting the personal information and privacy of affected residents; k) options for annual reporting to Council respecting the number, status, and resolution of groundwater interference complaints, trends, and mitigation measures undertaken by the Region; AND THAT staff include a transition provision allowing any resident who has submitted a groundwater interference complaint related to the K50, K51 and K52 wells since January 1, 2019, including residents who previously received a staff determination, compensation offer, denial, or release request, to request review through the new appeal process; AND THAT pending Council’s consideration of the revised policy, staff be directed not to require residents with active or unresolved complaints related to the K50, K51 and K52 wells to sign a full and final release as a condition of receiving temporary water support or emergency assistance; AND THAT staff report back with any legal, financial, staffing, procedural, privacy, and operational implications required to implement the revised process, including any amendments required to the current Policy and Procedures for Responding to Groundwater Interference Complaints or any related Regional policies.

Amendment

WHEREAS residents who rely on private wells must have access to a fair, transparent, evidence-based, and resident-centred process when they experience groundwater or surface water interference that may be connected to Regional water-taking activities;

AND WHEREAS the Region’s current Policy and Procedures for Responding to Groundwater Interference Complaints, revised in April 2015, provides for Regional staff to investigate complaints and provides that appeals are heard by the Commissioner of Transportation and Environmental Services (now interim Commissioner of Water Services and Wastewater Operations);

AND WHEREAS prior to the 2015 policy change, groundwater interference appeals in the Region of Waterloo were heard through a Council-appointed Well Interference Appeal Committee, formerly known as the Regional Water Liaison Committee;

AND WHEREAS residents have raised concerns that the current process does not provide sufficient independence, transparency, or meaningful appeal from staff determinations, particularly where the Region is both the operator of the municipal wells and the body responsible for investigating and deciding complaints related to those wells;

AND WHEREAS other Ontario municipalities, including the City of Guelph, maintain a Well Interference Committee model to hear appeals where a resident is dissatisfied with the municipality’s investigation, resolution, or compensation related to municipal groundwater taking;

AND WHEREAS the City of Guelph’s Well Interference Committee model provides for a committee to review staff investigations, hear directly from affected well owners, consider municipal pumping data and well information, and recommend restoration or additional restoration where appropriate;

AND WHEREAS the purpose of any well interference process should be to restore an adequate and reliable water supply to affected residents, rather than to limit the Region’s response to a fixed compensation amount that may not reflect the actual cost of restoration;

AND WHEREAS residents in the area of the K50, K51 and K52 wells have raised concerns regarding well interference and the impacts of increased or altered municipal pumping activity dating back to 2019;

AND WHEREAS residents in multiple areas of the Region have raised concerns regarding groundwater interference associated with municipal pumping activities;

AND WHEREAS public confidence in groundwater management is strengthened through transparent, evidence-based, and arms-length review processes;

THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT the Regional Municipality of Waterloo direct staff to bring forward a report and draft revised policy to the July 8th, 2026 Special Council Water meeting to replace the current groundwater interference appeal process with a Council-appointed Well Interference Appeal Committee;

AND THAT the revised policy and Terms of Reference be modelled on best practices from comparable municipal well interference appeal processes, including the City of Guelph model, and include the following:

  1.  a mandate for the Committee to hear appeals from private well owners regarding groundwater or surface water interference complaints related to Regional water-taking activities;
  2. a process for the Committee to be convened where Regional staff determine that the Region is not responsible for a well interference complaint, where a resident is dissatisfied with the resolution offered, or where a resident is dissatisfied with the amount or form of compensation offered;
  3. a membership model that includes members of Regional Council and representatives from affected lower-tier municipalities, with consideration given to independent hydrogeological or technical expertise;
  4. a requirement that members hearing an appeal be independent from the staff responsible for the original investigation and recommendation;
  5. a process that allows affected residents to provide written materials, attend the hearing, present evidence, respond to staff findings, and answer questions from the Committee;
  6. a requirement that the Committee review all relevant information, including the location of the affected well relative to Regional wells, private well depth and water levels, municipal well details, municipal pumping data, water-level monitoring data, complaint history, investigation findings, and any mitigation measures taken to date;
  7. authority for the Committee to make recommendations to Regional Council respecting appropriate remedies, including temporary water supply, pump lowering, well deepening, new well drilling, connection to municipal water where feasible, abandonment of the old well where required, reimbursement of eligible costs, or other measures necessary to restore a reliable water supply;
  8. options to remove or revise the current $4,000 compensation limit where the evidence supports greater actual costs to restore an adequate water supply;

i) options to ensure residents are not required to sign a full and final release of future claims before having access to a meaningful appeal process;

j) a transparent reporting process to Council, while protecting the personal information and privacy of affected residents;

j) enhanced public transparency respecting groundwater monitoring data, complaint tracking, investigation reporting, and Committee recommendations to Council, while protecting the personal information and privacy of affected residents;

k) options for annual reporting to Council respecting the number, status, and resolution of groundwater interference complaints, trends, and mitigation measures undertaken by the Region;

AND THAT staff include a transition provision allowing any resident who has submitted a groundwater or surface water interference complaint related to the K50, K51 and K52 wells since January 1, 2019, including residents who previously received a staff determination, compensation offer, denial, or release request, to request review through the new appeal process;

AND THAT pending Council’s consideration of the revised policy, staff be directed not to require residents with active or unresolved complaints related to the K50, K51 and K52 wells to sign a full and final release as a condition of receiving temporary water support or emergency assistance;

AND THAT staff report back with any legal, financial, staffing, procedural, privacy, and operational implications required to implement the revised process, including any amendments required to the currentPolicy and Procedures for Responding to Groundwater Interference Complaints or any related Regional policies.

Motion that may be Reconsidered

That the Regional Municipality of Waterloo approve the following as recommended by the external consultant, Mungall Consulting Group, for Council remuneration, benefits, and staff support during the 2026-2030 term of Council as outlined in PDL-CAS-26-009 dated April 22, 2026:

    1. Maintain the current practice of annual adjustments to the base compensation for the Regional Chair, Regional Councillor and Regional Standing Committee Chair, effective January 1 each year,
      1. by the average annual change in the all-items Consumer Price Index for Ontario for the previous year, not to exceed 3.0%.; and
      2. In years when Council has approved a freeze or austerity salary budget increase for Regional Municipality non-union staff, such Council-approved freeze or austerity increase shall extend to the approved increase for Regional Council members.
    2. Maintain components of total remuneration, including insured benefits and pension treatment; and
    3. Direct staff to include in the 2027 preliminary budget:
      1. one (1) additional Individual Contributor FTE to provide direct support to Regional Council members.
    4. And that the remuneration for Regional Standing Committee Chairs be increased from the current $7,401 to $12,901 annually, representing an approximate increase of $5500.00 (89%), for the 2026–2030 term of Council, and that this adjustment be incorporated into the 2027 budget.
